themes.title: Initialization and signal propagation
themes.summary: How the scale and structure of initial weights decide whether signals and gradients survive a forward and backward pass. This is the general deep-learning theory that RL initialization recipes build on.

themes.title: Policy-gradient implementation details
themes.summary: Large ablation studies of PPO-style agents, where small choices such as last-layer init, orthogonal weights, gradient clipping and advantage normalization turn out to matter as much as the algorithm.

themes.title: Value learning, divergence and the deadly triad
themes.summary: Why bootstrapped value learning with function approximation is fragile: divergence, overestimation, feature collapse, and the regularizers that counter them.

themes.title: Plasticity loss and dormant neurons
themes.summary: Networks trained on RL's shifting targets gradually lose the ability to fit new targets. This shows up as dormant neurons, collapsing feature rank, growing weight norms and sharp curvature.

themes.title: Resets and plasticity interventions
themes.summary: Remedies that partly re-initialize or re-randomize the network during training: full or partial resets, shrink-and-perturb, plasticity injection, continual backprop and regularizing toward the initialization.

themes.title: Normalization and architectures for stable scaling
themes.summary: Layer, batch, weight and spectral normalization, residual blocks and other architecture choices that let RL networks grow larger and train with higher replay ratios without diverging.

themes.title: Evaluation and reproducibility
themes.summary: How to tell whether a stability improvement is real: seed variance, confidence intervals and reporting practice.

papers.finding: Shows that with standard random init, activations and gradients shrink or saturate with depth (especially with sigmoid), and derives a fan-in/fan-out-balanced variance: the "Xavier" init.
papers.lesson: Weight variance should depend on layer width. This is the baseline idea behind every init scheme in the demo.
papers.title: Understanding the difficulty of training deep feedforward neural networks

papers.finding: Solves the learning dynamics of deep linear networks exactly and shows that random orthogonal initialization gives depth-independent learning times, unlike scaled Gaussian init.
papers.lesson: This is the theoretical root of the orthogonal init used in almost every PPO and A2C implementation.
papers.title: Exact solutions to the nonlinear dynamics of learning in deep linear neural networks

papers.finding: LSUV: start from orthogonal weights, then rescale each layer on a data batch so its output has unit variance.
papers.lesson: Data-dependent init is a cheap way to fix scale when analytic formulas don't match the architecture.
papers.title: All you need is a good init

papers.finding: Derives a weight variance of 2/fan_in that preserves activation variance through ReLU layers, which made very deep rectifier networks trainable from scratch.
papers.lesson: The right scale depends on the activation; ReLU networks need roughly twice the Xavier variance.
papers.title: Delving Deep into Rectifiers: Surpassing Human-Level Performance on ImageNet Classification

papers.finding: Shows that signals propagate only to a finite depth scale away from the order-to-chaos boundary, and networks deeper than that scale cannot be trained.
papers.lesson: Initializing at the "edge of chaos" is what makes depth trainable.
papers.title: Deep Information Propagation

papers.finding: Uses mean-field theory to show that random deep networks have an ordered and a chaotic phase, set by the weight and bias variances.
papers.lesson: Init variance moves a network between vanishing and exploding signal regimes. The signal-propagation explorer visualizes exactly this.
papers.title: Exponential expressivity in deep neural networks through transient chaos

papers.finding: Layer normalization normalizes each sample's activations across features, so it works with any batch size, and online.
papers.lesson: LayerNorm is now the most common stabilizer in RL networks because it doesn't depend on non-stationary batch statistics.
papers.title: Layer Normalization

papers.finding: Weight normalization reparameterizes each weight vector as a direction and a learned length, which decouples the norm from the direction and speeds optimization.
papers.lesson: Controlling weight norm explicitly reappears in recent RL work such as hyperspherical normalization and batch-plus-weight normalization.
papers.title: Weight Normalization: A Simple Reparameterization to Accelerate Training of Deep Neural Networks

papers.finding: Fixup rescales the initialization of residual branches, zero-initializing the last layer of each branch, so very deep residual networks train without normalization layers.
papers.lesson: Zero or small init of a branch's final layer makes each block start as the identity. RL's small policy-head init uses the same idea.
papers.title: Fixup Initialization: Residual Learning Without Normalization

papers.finding: Introduces the Maximal Update Parameterization (muP), which scales init and per-layer learning rates with width so features keep learning as width grows to infinity.
papers.lesson: Init scale and learning rate are coupled. A good scheme at one width can be wrong at another.
papers.title: Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks

papers.finding: Generalized Advantage Estimation is an exponentially weighted mix of n-step advantages, and lambda trades bias against variance.
papers.lesson: Lower-variance advantages make policy-gradient updates steadier. The demo uses GAE(0.95).
papers.title: High-Dimensional Continuous Control Using Generalized Advantage Estimation

papers.finding: Proximal Policy Optimization optimizes a clipped surrogate objective so it can take several minibatch epochs per batch while keeping each policy update small.
papers.lesson: PPO is the algorithm in the live demo. Its clipping is itself a stability mechanism.
papers.title: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms

papers.finding: Measures how far deep policy-gradient algorithms depart from the theory that motivates them: gradient estimates are poorly correlated with the true gradient and value baselines barely reduce variance.
papers.lesson: Noisy updates make training sensitive to scale and init. Stability tricks partly compensate for this noise.
papers.title: A Closer Look at Deep Policy Gradients

papers.finding: Shows that much of PPO's advantage over TRPO comes from code-level optimizations (orthogonal init, reward scaling, value clipping, learning-rate annealing), not from the clipped objective.
papers.lesson: Init and other unreported details can dominate algorithm comparisons.
papers.title: Implementation Matters in Deep Policy Gradients: A Case Study on PPO and TRPO

papers.finding: Trains more than 250,000 agents across implementation choices. One of the strongest recommendations: initialize the policy's last layer with weights about 100x smaller, so the initial action distribution is near-uniform and independent of the observation.
papers.lesson: This is direct evidence that output-layer init matters in on-policy RL. The demo's "Orthogonal + small heads" vs "no small heads" comparison reproduces it in miniature.
papers.title: What Matters In On-Policy Reinforcement Learning? A Large-Scale Empirical Study

papers.finding: Catalogs 37 implementation details of the reference PPO code, including orthogonal init with gain sqrt(2) for hidden layers, 0.01 for the policy head and 1 for the value head, plus Adam epsilon 1e-5 and global gradient clipping at 0.5.
papers.lesson: This is the source of the exact recipe in the demo's "Orthogonal + small heads" scheme.
papers.title: The 37 Implementation Details of Proximal Policy Optimization

papers.finding: Finds that in value-based agents the greedy policy changes on a large fraction of states after a single gradient step, and argues this churn acts as implicit exploration.
papers.lesson: Small updates can still cause large behavioral changes. Policy stability is not the same as parameter stability.
papers.title: The Phenomenon of Policy Churn

papers.finding: Studies plasticity loss in on-policy RL under distribution shift. Many methods that help off-policy agents fail here; regenerative methods such as shrink-and-perturb-style resets and regularization toward the initialization help.
papers.lesson: Interventions that keep the network close to a good initialization are a common thread.
papers.title: A Study of Plasticity Loss in On-Policy Deep Reinforcement Learning

papers.finding: Shows that PPO agents also lose plasticity: feature rank collapses over training, which then breaks the trust region. Proposes Proximal Feature Optimization, a regularizer on feature change.
papers.lesson: On-policy RL is not immune to plasticity loss. The demo tracks the actor's feature rank for this reason.
papers.title: No Representation, No Trust: Connecting Representation, Collapse, and Trust Issues in PPO

papers.finding: Deep Q-Networks learned Atari from pixels, using experience replay to stabilize Q-learning with a convolutional network.
papers.lesson: Replay buffers, and later target networks, were the first stability fixes for deep value learning.
papers.title: Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning

papers.finding: TD3 counters overestimation bias in actor-critic methods with clipped double-Q learning, delayed policy updates and target policy smoothing.
papers.lesson: Value-estimation error compounds through bootstrapping. Stability comes from controlling it.
papers.title: Addressing Function Approximation Error in Actor-Critic Methods

papers.finding: Empirically studies the deadly triad (function approximation, bootstrapping, off-policy learning) in DQN variants. Unbounded divergence is rare, but soft divergence is common and depends on target networks, multi-step returns and prioritization.
papers.lesson: Divergence risk is a measurable function of design choices, not a fixed fact of the algorithm.
papers.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning and the Deadly Triad

papers.finding: Soft Actor-Critic is an off-policy maximum-entropy actor-critic method that is notably more stable across seeds than earlier off-policy methods.
papers.lesson: An entropy bonus keeps the policy from collapsing early, much like the small policy-head init does at step zero.
papers.title: Soft Actor-Critic: Off-Policy Maximum Entropy Deep Reinforcement Learning with a Stochastic Actor

papers.finding: Shows that bootstrapped value learning progressively reduces the effective rank (srank) of learned features, and that this rank collapse correlates with poor performance.
papers.lesson: Introduces the srank metric that the demo plots as "feature rank".
papers.title: Implicit Under-Parameterization Inhibits Data-Efficient Deep Reinforcement Learning

papers.finding: Finds that TD-trained networks show lower interference between states and worse generalization than regression-trained ones, and links this to how targets evolve over training.
papers.lesson: How the targets are produced shapes the representation the network learns.
papers.title: Interference and Generalization in Temporal Difference Learning

papers.finding: Disentangles replay capacity from the age of the oldest policy in the buffer, and shows that n-step returns are key to benefiting from larger replay.
papers.lesson: Replay ratio and data age are stability levers as important as the network itself.
papers.title: Revisiting Fundamentals of Experience Replay

papers.finding: DR3 identifies implicit regularization in TD learning that makes features of consecutive state-action pairs co-adapt, and adds an explicit regularizer on their dot product.
papers.lesson: Value-based RL needs explicit regularization that supervised learning does not.
papers.title: DR3: Value-Based Deep Reinforcement Learning Requires Explicit Regularization

papers.finding: The tandem experiment: a passive agent trained on exactly the same data as an active agent still fails badly. The paper traces this mainly to function approximation interacting with the data distribution.
papers.lesson: Identical data and objectives can still give very different results: optimization dynamics matter, not only the data.
papers.title: The Difficulty of Passive Learning in Deep Reinforcement Learning

papers.finding: At high update-to-data ratios, the main failure is not the primacy bias but divergence of Q-values driven by out-of-distribution action prediction. Normalizing the output features fixes much of it without resets.
papers.lesson: Some failures that resets were fixing can be prevented by architecture instead.
papers.title: Dissecting Deep RL with High Update Ratios: Combatting Value Divergence

papers.finding: Proves that LayerNorm plus L2 regularization makes TD learning stable even off-policy, and builds PQN: a Q-learning agent with no target network or replay buffer, running in vectorized environments.
papers.lesson: Normalization can replace target networks as a stabilizer, which is a strong argument for architecture-level fixes.
papers.title: Simplifying Deep Temporal Difference Learning

papers.finding: Training value functions with a cross-entropy loss over binned returns (HL-Gauss) instead of MSE regression scales better and is more robust to noisy targets.
papers.lesson: Changing the loss's geometry can remove a whole class of value-learning instabilities.
papers.title: Stop Regressing: Training Value Functions via Classification for Scalable Deep RL

papers.finding: Shows that transient non-stationarity early in RL training permanently hurts generalization. ITER periodically distills the agent into a freshly initialized network.
papers.lesson: Re-initializing and distilling can undo damage that early training left behind.
papers.title: Transient Non-Stationarity and Generalisation in Deep Reinforcement Learning

papers.finding: Shows that networks trained on sequences of targets lose capacity to fit new ones, measured by feature rank. InFeR regresses some outputs toward their values at initialization to preserve capacity.
papers.lesson: Staying close to initialization's function preserves plasticity, which makes the init a resource to protect.
papers.title: Understanding and Preventing Capacity Loss in Reinforcement Learning

papers.finding: DrM shows that the dormant ratio in visual RL agents tracks exploration and performance, and uses it to drive perturbation, exploration and exploitation schedules.
papers.lesson: Network-health metrics can act as control signals, not just diagnostics.
papers.title: DrM: Mastering Visual Reinforcement Learning through Dormant Ratio Minimization

papers.finding: Shows plasticity loss in continual deep RL on Atari and connects it to activation-footprint changes. Concatenated ReLUs (CReLU) mitigate it.
papers.lesson: Activation choice affects how quickly units die. The demo lets you switch tanh and ReLU.
papers.title: Loss of Plasticity in Continual Deep Reinforcement Learning

papers.finding: Demonstrates large-scale loss of plasticity under continual learning with standard deep learning (including on ImageNet-derived tasks and in RL) and proposes continual backpropagation, which keeps re-initializing a small fraction of low-utility units.
papers.lesson: Initialization is not a one-time event. Injecting fresh random units keeps a network trainable.
papers.title: Maintaining Plasticity in Deep Continual Learning

papers.finding: Separates input plasticity (adapting to new inputs) from label plasticity (adapting to new targets) and combines SAM, LayerNorm, CReLU and resets in PLASTIC.
papers.lesson: Different remedies target different parts of the problem, so they combine well.
papers.title: PLASTIC: Improving Input and Label Plasticity for Sample Efficient Reinforcement Learning

papers.finding: Defines tau-dormant neurons (normalized mean activation at or below tau) and shows their fraction grows during deep RL training. ReDo recycles them by re-initializing their incoming weights and zeroing their outgoing weights.
papers.lesson: The demo's dormant-fraction chart uses this definition directly.
papers.title: The Dormant Neuron Phenomenon in Deep Reinforcement Learning

papers.finding: Finds that plasticity loss is best explained by changes in loss-landscape curvature rather than by weight norm or rank alone, and shows LayerNorm is a strong mitigation.
papers.lesson: No single scalar metric predicts plasticity loss. The demo plots several for this reason.
papers.title: Understanding plasticity in neural networks

papers.finding: Disentangles several independent causes of plasticity loss (preactivation shift, unit saturation and dormancy, growing parameter norms) and shows that layer normalization plus weight decay together are robust across settings.
papers.lesson: Combine a normalization layer with norm control instead of looking for a single fix.
papers.title: Disentangling the Causes of Plasticity Loss in Neural Networks

papers.finding: Shows that with normalization layers, growing parameter norms silently shrink the effective learning rate. Normalize-and-Project keeps the effective step size constant.
papers.lesson: The weight-norm chart in the demo is about this effect, which is invisible in the loss curve.
papers.title: Normalization and effective learning rates in reinforcement learning

papers.finding: Adam combines momentum with per-parameter adaptive step sizes from bias-corrected first and second moment estimates.
papers.lesson: Adam's epsilon and moment state interact with init scale. RL code commonly uses epsilon = 1e-5, as the demo does.
papers.title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization

papers.finding: Warm-starting from a model trained on part of the data generalizes worse than training from scratch. Shrink-and-perturb (scale weights down, add noise) recovers most of the gap.
papers.lesson: Partially moving weights back toward a random init is a simple, general plasticity fix.
papers.title: On Warm-Starting Neural Network Training

papers.finding: Shows that repeatedly forgetting and relearning, by resetting later layers, steers networks toward better generalizing solutions.
papers.lesson: Controlled re-initialization can act as a regularizer.
papers.title: Fortuitous Forgetting in Connectionist Networks

papers.finding: Identifies the primacy bias, a tendency to overfit early experience, and shows that periodically resetting the last layers of the network, while keeping the replay buffer, improves sample efficiency substantially.
papers.lesson: Re-initialization during training can beat continuous training. This is the foundation for most later reset work.
papers.title: The Primacy Bias in Deep Reinforcement Learning

papers.finding: Bigger, Better, Faster reaches human-level Atari 100k performance by scaling the network, using shrink-and-perturb resets, annealing n-step and discount, and using weight decay.
papers.lesson: Resets are what make larger networks and high replay ratios usable.
papers.title: Bigger, Better, Faster: Human-level Atari with human-level efficiency

papers.finding: Plasticity injection adds a freshly initialized copy of the head and subtracts a frozen copy, so plasticity increases without changing the network's current output or adding trainable parameters permanently.
papers.lesson: Fresh random weights can be added without a performance drop.
papers.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning with Plasticity Injection

papers.finding: L2 Init regularizes parameters toward their initial values instead of toward zero, maintaining plasticity in continual learning more simply than resets.
papers.lesson: The initial weights are a good anchor to return to.
papers.title: Maintaining Plasticity in Continual Learning via Regenerative Regularization

papers.finding: Resetting Adam's moment estimates whenever the target network updates significantly improves Rainbow on Atari, because stale moments from earlier targets corrupt new updates.
papers.lesson: Optimizer state is part of what has to be re-initialized.
papers.title: Resetting the Optimizer in Deep RL: An Empirical Study

papers.finding: Utility-based perturbed gradient descent protects useful units and perturbs less useful ones, addressing both plasticity loss and catastrophic forgetting.
papers.lesson: Targeted, utility-aware perturbation beats uniform resets when old knowledge matters.
papers.title: Addressing Loss of Plasticity and Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Learning

papers.finding: Spectral regularization keeps each layer's largest singular value near 1, preserving the gradient-propagation properties of the initialization and so maintaining trainability over long task sequences.
papers.lesson: Instead of resetting weights, preserve the property of the initialization that matters: its spectrum.
papers.title: Learning Continually by Spectral Regularization

papers.finding: Models parameter drift toward the initialization as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with a learned drift rate, which gives soft, adaptive resets under non-stationarity.
papers.lesson: Reset strength can be learned instead of scheduled by hand.
papers.title: Non-Stationary Learning of Neural Networks with Automatic Soft Parameter Reset

papers.finding: Feeds the state input into every hidden layer (dense connections), which helps deeper actor-critic networks train in continuous control.
papers.lesson: Skip connections ease the gradient-flow problems that limit depth in RL.
papers.title: D2RL: Deep Dense Architectures in Reinforcement Learning

papers.finding: Shows that spectral normalization's benefit in DQN-style agents comes mostly from its effect on optimization (an effective step size), not from smoothness. Proposes cheaper alternatives.
papers.lesson: Many stabilizers work by changing effective learning rates.
papers.title: Spectral Normalisation for Deep Reinforcement Learning: an Optimisation Perspective

papers.finding: Spectral normalization lets much deeper and wider networks be used in SAC-style agents, where unnormalized large networks would otherwise destabilize.
papers.lesson: Smoothness constraints, not just init, unlock depth in RL.
papers.title: Towards Deeper Deep Reinforcement Learning with Spectral Normalization

papers.finding: Shows that naively enlarging RL networks hurts, and gets gains by decoupling representation learning from RL and using DenseNet-style connections plus distributed training.
papers.lesson: Scaling RL networks needs both architecture and training-procedure changes.
papers.title: Training Larger Networks for Deep Reinforcement Learning

papers.finding: DreamerV3 masters over 150 tasks with fixed hyperparameters using robustness techniques such as symlog predictions, LayerNorm, return normalization and zero-initialized output layers for some heads.
papers.lesson: One set of hyperparameters can work everywhere once scale is controlled at every interface.
papers.title: Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models

papers.finding: BRO scales the critic with LayerNorm and residual blocks, uses strong regularization and resets, and adds optimistic exploration, reaching state-of-the-art continuous control.
papers.lesson: Scaling up only works once normalization and resets keep training stable.
papers.title: Bigger, Regularized, Optimistic: scaling for compute and sample-efficient continuous control

papers.finding: CrossQ removes target networks and uses carefully applied batch normalization, joint forward passes of current and next states and wider critics, matching REDQ/DroQ sample efficiency at a low update ratio.
papers.lesson: With the right normalization, the classic stabilizers (target nets, high UTD) can be dropped.
papers.title: CrossQ: Batch Normalization in Deep Reinforcement Learning for Greater Sample Efficiency and Simplicity

papers.finding: Gradual magnitude pruning makes value-based agents perform better as networks grow, where dense scaling usually hurts.
papers.lesson: Bigger dense networks are harder to keep stable in RL, so sparsity is an alternative route.
papers.title: In value-based deep reinforcement learning, a pruned network is a good network

papers.finding: Soft mixture-of-experts layers in value-based agents give performance that improves with parameter count, along with fewer dormant neurons and more stable feature rank.
papers.lesson: Architecture changes show up directly in the plasticity metrics.
papers.title: Mixtures of Experts Unlock Parameter Scaling for Deep RL

papers.finding: Benchmarks over 60 off-policy agents built from combinations of regularization and plasticity interventions across 14 tasks. Generic network regularization such as LayerNorm, together with resets, does as well as RL-specific tricks.
papers.lesson: Practical RL stability benefits most from standard deep-learning regularizers.
papers.title: Overestimation, Overfitting, and Plasticity in Actor-Critic: the Bitter Lesson of Reinforcement Learning

papers.finding: SimBa combines running observation normalization, residual feedforward blocks and LayerNorm. The result has a simplicity bias that lets RL networks scale up in parameters without losing performance.
papers.lesson: The architecture's inductive bias, not only its init, decides whether bigger networks help in RL.
papers.title: SimBa: Simplicity Bias for Scaling Up Parameters in Deep Reinforcement Learning

papers.finding: SimbaV2 constrains weights and features to a hypersphere and uses distributional value estimation with reward scaling, which keeps effective learning rates stable as models and compute scale.
papers.lesson: Projecting weights onto a fixed norm directly removes the growing-weight-norm failure mode.
papers.title: Hyperspherical Normalization for Scalable Deep Reinforcement Learning

papers.finding: Adds weight normalization to CrossQ so it scales reliably to higher update-to-data ratios without resets.
papers.lesson: Norm control on weights complements batch normalization on activations.
papers.title: Scaling Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning with Batch and Weight Normalization

papers.finding: Attributes the failure of naively scaled deep RL networks to non-stationarity combined with poor gradient flow, and stabilizes scaling with gradient-propagation-preserving architecture and optimizer changes.
papers.lesson: Signal propagation, the theme of the first section, returns as the main issue at scale.
papers.title: Stable Gradients for Stable Learning at Scale in Deep Reinforcement Learning

papers.finding: Shows that deep RL results vary hugely with random seeds, hyperparameters, network architecture and code base, so reported improvements are often not significant.
papers.lesson: Init effects must be judged across many seeds. The demo runs several seeds per scheme and shades their range.
papers.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning that Matters

papers.finding: Argues that point estimates from few runs mislead, and recommends interquartile mean, stratified bootstrap confidence intervals and performance profiles (the rliable library).
papers.lesson: Report intervals over seeds, not single curves.
papers.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning at the Edge of the Statistical Precipice
